summary: Learners move fluently in BOTH directions between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate these on a 0–1 number line. The skill rests on place-value meaning — the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths — so the denominator is read from the final place (10 → one place, 100 → two places), and a placeholder zero is needed when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). Learning and checking should deliberately use placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases, because a digit-copying rule produces correct answers on easy items but fails exactly there.
misconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero: writing 9/100 as 0.9, or reading 0.07 as 7/10.
Adding an unneeded zero: writing 3/10 as 0.03 by over-applying 'hundredths = two places'.
Using one denominator for every decimal: writing 0.4 as 4/100 regardless of the number of places.
Reversing digits or reading position wrong: 0.62 → 6/2 or 26/100.
Placing decimals on the number line by whole-number reasoning rather than by tenths/hundredths.

activities.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
steps: Enter a decimal (e.g. 0.62) and write the matching fraction; confirm against a 10×10 hundredths grid that shades 62 squares and a number-line marker that lands just past halfway.
Enter a fraction (e.g. 3/10) and write the matching decimal (0.3); confirm by shading 3 of the ten columns and placing the point on the line.
Do the hard placeholder case: for 9/100, if you write 0.9 the grid floods with ninety squares — far more than nine — so the mismatch is obvious; correct it to 0.09 so exactly nine squares glow.
Run rapid two-way rounds (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) across a deliberate set of placeholder and ragged cases: 0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100.
Read each decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths', 'seven hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
activities.insight: The placeholder zero is not a rule to memorise but something you can see: for 9/100 the zero keeps the nine out of the tenths place. The denominator is determined by the final decimal place, and every symbolic answer can be checked against a shaded quantity and a position on the line.

activities.title: Contrast sets that drill the placeholder
steps: Work matched pairs side by side: {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07}, writing each as both a fraction and a decimal.
For each pair, shade a hundredths grid for both members so the size difference is visible (3 columns vs 3 squares; 70 squares vs 7 squares).
State in words why one needs a placeholder zero and the other does not.
Sort a mixed set of cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other) and self-check by flipping, giving special attention to 0.4, 0.07 and 9/100.
activities.insight: Tenths and hundredths of the same digit look similar in writing but differ ten-fold in size; the number of decimal places and the presence of a placeholder zero both follow from which place the final digit occupies.

activities.title: Annotated place-value chart as a reference (scaffold)
steps: Study a place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside a couple of worked conversions, e.g. 0.62 = 62/100 and 9/100 = 0.09.
Read a short explanation of why the placeholder zero appears in 0.09 but not in 0.3.
Return to the converter or contrast-set tasks and reproduce the method on new values without looking.
activities.insight: A worked reference makes the place–denominator link and the placeholder rule explicit, but fluency comes from doing many items, not from reading examples.

checkQuestion: Write these decimals as fractions: 0.62, 0.07, 0.4. Now write these as decimals: 3/10, 9/100. Last, mark 0.4 on this number line from 0 to 1. Show me how you work each one out.
